procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 21.03.2011 of the High Court of Andhra Pradesh at Hyderabad in CRLA No.54 of 2005.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant preferred an appeal before the High Court against the judgment of conviction and sentence passed by the Trial Court. The High Court reappreciated the evidence on record and confirmed the conviction and sentence recorded by the Trial Court.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The original appellant P. Sarangapani died pending the appeal. His wife, Paka Saroja, was permitted to proceed with the appeal. The Supreme Court found the criminal appeal devoid of merits and dismissed it.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justiﬁ ed in conﬁ rming the conviction of appellant-accused no.1 u/s. 7 and s.13(1)(d) r/w 13(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988.

facts: The appellant, a Sub Registrar of Cooperative Societies, was accused of demanding and accepting a bribe of Rs. 1,500 from a complainant.
The alleged bribe was for an official favour: allowing the complainant to continue as the President of a society.
The Trial Court convicted the appellant under Sections 7 and 13(1)(d) read with 13(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988.
The High Court re-examined the evidence and confirmed the Trial Court's conviction and sentence.
The appellant then appealed to the Supreme Court, arguing that the prosecution had failed to prove the demand for the bribe, especially since the original complainant had died before the trial.
law: Under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, Section 7 criminalizes a public servant accepting gratification other than legal remuneration as a motive or reward for an official act.
Section 13(1)(d) defines criminal misconduct by a public servant.

Section 20 of the Act establishes a statutory presumption. If it is proven that an accused has accepted gratification (other than legal remuneration), the court must presume it was accepted as an illegal motive or reward, unless the accused proves the contrary. This presumption is rebuttable.
application: The Supreme Court first noted that both the Trial Court and the High Court had thoroughly appreciated the evidence and reached the same conclusion (concurrent findings), and it saw no valid reason to interfere with these well-considered findings.

The Court found that the prosecution had successfully proven the foundational facts of the case, including the pre-trap and post-trap proceedings, the "conscious acceptance of the tainted currency by the accused," and the recovery of that money from him.
By proving the acceptance and recovery of the money, the prosecution triggered the statutory presumption under Section 20 of the Act.
This shifted the burden of proof to the appellant to show that he had accepted the money for a legitimate reason and not as a bribe.
The appellant offered an explanation that the money was for the Society's "Audit fees." However, the Court held that the appellant failed to prove this defense.
The Court also noted that the explanation offered by the appellant was not consistent with the statement the complainant had previously given under Section 164 of the Cr.P.C.
Therefore, the appellant failed to rebut the legal presumption that the money was accepted as an illegal gratification.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court was justified in confirming the conviction. It found no reason to interfere with the concurrent findings of the lower courts, as the prosecution had proven the acceptance of the bribe, thereby shifting the burden to the appellant under Section 20 of the Act, a burden which the appellant failed to discharge.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justiﬁ ed in conﬁ rming the conviction of appellant-accused no.1 u/s. 7 and s.13(1)(d) r/w 13(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988.
appellant_arguments: The prosecution failed to prove the essential element of demand for illegal gratification, which is a prerequisite for conviction.
Since the complainant died before the trial and could not be examined, the allegation of demand was not proven beyond a reasonable doubt.
In the absence of proof of demand, the statutory presumption of guilt under Section 20 of the Prevention of Corruption Act cannot be drawn against the accused.
The complainant's own statement, recorded under Section 164 of the Cr.P.C., indicated that the amount paid was for the society's audit fees, not a bribe.
The complainant's statement also suggested that the appellant was falsely implicated by a former President of the society who held a grudge against him.
respondent_arguments: The death of the complainant is not fatal to the prosecution's case, as the charges can be established through other oral and documentary evidence.
The prosecution successfully proved the pre-trap and post-trap proceedings by examining other witnesses who supported its case.
The prosecution proved the conscious acceptance and recovery of the tainted currency from the appellant.
Once acceptance and recovery were proven, the burden shifted to the appellant under the statutory presumption in Section 20 of the Act to prove the money was not a bribe, which he failed to do.

The appellant's defense that the money was for audit fees was not substantiated, as there was no record showing the money came from the society's funds, and this explanation was inconsistent with the complainant's statement.

cases.case_name: Neeraj Dutta vs. State (Government of NCT of Delhi)
cases.principle: Once the acceptance of an undue advantage is proved, the court is entitled to raise the rebuttable presumption under Section 20 of the Prevention of Corruption Act that the accused accepted it as a motive or reward for performing a public duty improperly or dishonestly.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The death or non-availability of a complainant during trial is not fatal to the prosecution's case, nor is it a ground for acquittal, as the prosecution may prove the complaint and other facts through other oral or documentary evidence.
obiter: Under Section 7 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, upon proof of the foundational facts, Section 20 mandates the court to raise a legal presumption that the illegal gratification was for a motive or reward, which is subject to rebuttal by the accused.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: Once the prosecution proved the conscious acceptance and recovery of the tainted currency from the appellant, the burden shifted to the appellant under the statutory presumption in Section 20 of the Prevention of Corruption Act. The appellant failed to dispel this presumption by proving, on a preponderance of probability, that the money was not accepted as a motive or reward for the performance of his public duty, as his explanation that the money was for audit fees was unsubstantiated and inconsistent with the complainant's statement.
legal_tests_applied: Once the undue advantage i.e., any gratiﬁcation whatever, other than the legal remuneration is proved to have been accepted by the accused, the Court is entitled to raise the presumption u/s. 20 that he accepted the undue advantage as a motive or reward u/s. 7 for performing or to cause performance of a public duty improperly or dishonestly.
The death of the complainant or non-availability of the complainant at the time of trial would not be fatal to the case of the prosecution.
The accused is not required to establish his defence beyond reasonable doubt as the prosecution, and can establish the same on the preponderance of probability.
The statutory presumption under Section 20 is rebuttable.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant failed to dispel the statutory presumption u/s. 20 of the said Act, and prove that it was not accepted as a motive or reward for the performance of his public duty.
The explanation oﬀered by the appellant did not tally with the statement of the complainant recorded u/s. 164 of Cr.PC.

The defence taken by the appellant that the acceptance of tainted currency by him was towards the Audit fees of the Society was not proved by him in as much as there was nothing on record to show that the amount paid by the complainant to the appellant was out of the funds of the Society.
why_respondent_won: The pre-trap and post-trap proceedings were duly proved by the prosecution by examining the concerned witnesses, who had duly supported the case of prosecution.
The prosecution had proved beyond reasonable doubt the conscious acceptance of the tainted currency by the accused and also the recovery of tainted currency from the appellant.
By proving acceptance and recovery, the burden shifted on the appellant to dispel the statutory presumption u/s. 20 of the said Act.
